power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Distinguishing problematic from non-problematic chemsex, or placing experience on a continuum of severity, generates limited information about why similar drug use can lead to different experiences and support needs.
We propose considering how the circumstances of an encounter work together and change over time.

Method: This think piece presents a selective conceptual synthesis of chemsex research and assessment approaches, informed by minority stress theory, drug, set and setting, functional analysis, and addiction science.
Empirical studies inform the domains and the proposed relationships between them.
Results: Six questions (who, what, why, with, where and when) describe the person, substances, functions, relationships, settings and timing within a changing chemsex configuration.
Digital activity may connect these through partner contact, planning and support, and is an important emerging consideration.
Three fictional vignettes illustrate different responses to comparable exposure.
The person and therapist could each map the configuration, compare accounts and identify a focus for formulation and therapy.
Conclusions: Assessment should determine how pleasure, protection and harm arise through interacting circumstances.
The six Ws direct attention to these relationships and to differences between the person's and therapist's accounts.
Participatory development and longitudinal evaluation are needed to establish whether this approach improves shared understanding, decisions and care.
Chemsex describes the intentional use of particular psychoactive substances before or during sexual activity to facilitate, intensify or prolong the experience.

In the United Kingdom, the term emerged within men who have sex with me (MSM) communities and commonly refers to methamphetamine, synthetic cathinones (mostly mephedrone, 4-MMC) and gamma-hydroxybutyrate or gamma-butyrolactone (GHB/GBL), although sessions may involve other drugs (McCall et al., 2015; Stuart, 2019).

The following fictional vignettes illustrate how the configuration might guide clinical work.
Each involves stimulant and GHB/GBL use in overnight sexual settings, which in itself may be an oversimplification of the heterogeneity of chemsex presentations in practice..
In the first, a man plans infrequent sessions with a trusted network for pleasure and exploration.
He measures doses, avoids injecting, discusses consent and protects the following day for recovery.
Acute drug risks remain.
Support could reinforce overdose precautions and recovery while considering what might disrupt these protections.
In the second, a man seeks connection when social anxiety is high.
He meets unfamiliar partners through apps, struggles to hold boundaries under intoxication and follows further invitations as sessions extend.
Dosing is similar to the first example, but support may focus on consent, an exit plan, app boundaries and other routes to connection.
In the third, a man describes trauma-related distress, loneliness and chronic sleep loss.
Reactive dosing includes injecting methamphetamine, and closely spaced sessions span several different chemsex settings.
He seeks relief rather than exploration and reports intense shame afterwards.
Acute safety, sleep, nutrition and continuity of care take priority.
Trauma-informed work and alternatives can follow as stability improves, alongside urgent medical or safeguarding action when indicated.
Support needs to address the relief chemsex offers as well as its costs.
The framework's main proposition is that domains modify one another.
The same exposure may have different consequences depending on relationships, motives and recovery; the same person may move between configurations without increasing drug use.
A familiar home might support safety while carrying powerful cues, just as a trusted network might offer care while increasing access to substances.
Whether a component protects, harms or does both depends on its place within the configuration.
Clinically, the configuration offers a way to identify where help might be useful.

The clinical usefulness of the six Ws requires evaluation and this model is not empirically supported.
Rather, it brings together strands of evidence within the literature and synthesises them into a new way of considering chemsex now, versus then.
Participatory work should include people whose experiences are pleasurable, ambivalent or harmful, including those outside treatment.

Community organisations and practitioners can examine missing content, acceptability and feasibility, including whether comparing maps helps people and therapists agree a useful focus and improve care.
Repeated assessments before and after sessions could test whether distress, partner familiarity and recovery plans explain outcomes beyond drug exposure and frequency.
Digital measures should distinguish passive content exposure, active searching and direct invitations, recording their timing relative to urges and use.
This could help establish whether online contact precedes change or reflects existing intention.
Analyses should test specified interactions and include agency, pleasure and connection alongside adverse events.
Recurring configurations would describe relationships that may change over time.
Limitations The literature uses uneven definitions and often relies on convenience samples and cross-sectional self-report.
The six labels overlap and may compress structural or biological influences.
Their proposed clinical use needs testing, particularly whether exploring relationships between domains changes the priorities identified through assessment.
Assessment also depends on trust and what can be communicated.
Embodied pleasure or implicit learning may be difficult to describe, and people may reasonably withhold information from services.
The literature centres on gay and bisexual men; use with other communities requires development with them and attention to the terms they use.
Criminalisation, discrimination and inaccessible services also require action beyond individual clinical work.
